## Question

Same question as the superseded entry: should wildfire build on TensorRT-LLM?
It is revisited within the hour because the first answer leaned on precedent,
and precedent is not evidence. Wildfire's premise is that the target — a 321B
sparse MoE at 4-bit serving interactively from two 128 GB boxes — is reachable
precisely because nobody has bothered. An engine built on that premise cannot
reject its own dependencies for being unsupported.

## What was wrong with the first answer

Two of the four objections were about what has been done, not what can be done,
and one was simply false.

- **"Not in the model zoo" is not a barrier.** Plugins and custom model
  definitions exist. The absence of GLM-5.3-Flash means work, not impossibility.
- **"`sm_121` coverage is unproven" is a build flag.** `build_wheel.py` accepts
  `--cuda_architectures`, so `121-real` is something to compile, not something
  to wait for. The published support matrix describes what NVIDIA ships, not
  what the source can target.
- **"Closed kernels" was wrong.** `cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels` has 167 entries in
  the open. TensorRT — the graph optimization library — is the closed component;
  TensorRT-LLM is a different thing, and its PyTorch backend path does not build
  TensorRT engines at all. Conflating them was an error.

## What survives

One objection is not about difficulty, and it is the one that decides this:
**what does adopting the runtime contribute, given we implement KDA, DSA and the
4-bit grouped expert GEMM ourselves either way?**

| Component it offers | What we would actually do |
| --- | --- |
| Tuned kernels for supported layers | Our hot layers are not among them; we write KDA, DSA, grouped MoE regardless |
| Batch manager and scheduler | Replaced — expert-affinity batching and decode priority are [scheduler](../../design.qmd#scheduler) decisions |
| Graph runtime | Shapes are static by doctrine; CUDA graphs over our own launcher is a small component |
| KV cache manager | Must be replaced — the atomic `(KV, KDA)` entry in the [state cache](../../design.qmd#cache) is the entire point |

Adoption costs a maintained fork of a large, fast-moving C++ codebase and
returns the component we need least. That is a value argument, and it survives
someone willing to do arbitrary amounts of work.

## Verdict

**The runtime is rejected on contribution, not on difficulty.** Wildfire's
compiler and runtime stay ours.

**The kernels are explicitly not rejected.** The superseded entry treated
"TRT-LLM kernels may not run on `sm_121`" as a reason to stop looking. It is
instead an experiment, now registered as open:

> Build TensorRT-LLM from source with `--cuda_architectures=121-real` on the
> head node, and microbenchmark its NVFP4 grouped-expert GEMM and sparse-MLA
> kernels against ours on GB10. If they win, link or port them.

Consuming a kernel does not require adopting a runtime, and this is the version
of the question that can actually be answered with a number.
